204.title: Legion (Mark 5:1–20)
204.hook: a man living in tombs is freed and asks to follow; go home and tell your friends
204.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of the Gerasene man in the weekday Mass readings; the Church's rite of exorcism is reserved to a priest with the bishop's permission and requires that medical and psychological causes be ruled out first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace, be still, and a calmed sea. Your line was who is this. Today, the boat lands on the other side, and you find out what the storm was crossing toward.

The boat scrapes onto a beach on the far side of the lake. A great herd of swine feeds on the hillside, a sign, some readers note, of Gentile country. Before Jesus is even out of the boat, a man comes running at him from the graveyard. He lives there, among the tombs. People have tried to chain him, and he's snapped the chains. Day and night he's out in the hills, crying out and cutting himself with stones. Nobody can hold him. Nobody goes near.
screen: `THE FAR SIDE OF THE LAKE.` → `A MAN AMONG THE TOMBS.` → `NO CHAIN CAN HOLD HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Jesus asks him, what is thy name? The answer comes, in the Douay-Rheims: "My name is Legion, for we are many." A legion was a unit of the Roman army, so the name says: I'm not one person anymore. I'm occupied. Some readers hear in it Rome's own legions, occupying the land. Second, the pigs. The spirits beg to be sent into the herd, about two thousand, Mark says, and the herd rushes down the steep bank into the sea. It's a strange scene, and the gospel doesn't explain it. Third, the town. The herdsmen run and tell everyone. People come out and find the man sitting there, clothed, in his right mind. And they're afraid, not of the storm or the demons now, but of Jesus. They beg him to leave. Fourth, the surprise. As Jesus gets into the boat, the healed man begs to go with him. Jesus has been calling followers all along. This time he says no. "Go into thy house to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had mercy on thee." So the man becomes a messenger in his own country, telling through the Decapolis what Jesus had done for him, and all marvel. One note of care: the gospel speaks of unclean spirits. Catholics don't read it as saying that mental illness is demonic; the Church asks that illness be treated by medicine.

205.title: The story inside the story (Mark 5:21–43)
205.hook: Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus's daughter; both are daughters
205.howItsDone: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter and the healing of the woman at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and the Church prays for the sick through the sacrament of anointing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Legion: a man freed and sent home. Your line was go home and tell. Today Jesus crosses back.

A father falls at a teacher's feet, begging him to come: his little girl is dying. They set off through a pressing crowd, and every minute counts. And then the teacher stops. Mark does something you saw on day two hundred: he starts one story, stops it halfway, tells a whole second story in the middle, and only then finishes the first. Scholars call it a Markan sandwich. And the two stories turn out to be mirrors of each other.
screen: `A FATHER BEGS: COME QUICKLY.` → `THE TEACHER STOPS.` → `A MARKAN SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: First, the outside story. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, an important man, falls at Jesus's feet. My little daughter is dying, he says; come and lay your hands on her. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses in around him. Second, the inside story. In that crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything on doctors and only got worse, and under the law the bleeding also kept her ritually unclean. She thinks: if I can just touch his clothes. She does, and she feels it: she's healed. And Jesus stops. "Who hath touched my garments?" The disciples point out the obvious: the whole crowd is pressing on you. Meanwhile Jairus stands there, his daughter dying, and Jesus waits. The woman comes forward, trembling, and tells him the whole truth. He says: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Third, the bad news. While he's still speaking, messengers arrive: your daughter is dead; why trouble the master any further? Jesus turns to Jairus: "Fear not, only believe." At the house, he takes the girl by the hand and says: talitha cumi. Mark keeps the words as Jesus said them, then translates: damsel, arise. She gets up and walks, and Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. Fourth, the mirrors. The woman has been sick twelve years; the girl is twelve years old. Both are called daughter. Both are unclean by the law, one bleeding, one dead. She touches him; he takes the girl by the hand. And the interruption that looked like it cost the girl her life turns out to be part of the same healing.

206.title: The carpenter (Mark 6:1–6)
206.hook: at home they say isn't this the carpenter, and he could do few miracles there
206.howItsDone: Catholics honor Jesus's years of ordinary work in Nazareth, especially on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, and some offer their daily work as a prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, talitha cumi: two daughters, one healing. Your line was interruptions are the ministry. Today Jesus goes home.

Nazareth. A small place, where people have known each other a long time. The neighbors remember the boy, the workshop, the family. Jesus has been teaching, healing and calming storms around the lake, with crowds following. Now he comes home. And home has already decided who he is. Going back to the place that knew you first can mean being seen as who you were, not who you've become.
screen: `A HOMETOWN THAT REMEMBERS.` → `WHO YOU WERE.` → `JESUS GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the question. On the sabbath he teaches in the synagogue, and people are astonished. Where did he get all this? What's this wisdom? Then the astonishment curdles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary". They list his brothers by name and say his sisters are right here with us. And they were scandalized, Mark says: they stumbled over him. Second, the word carpenter. Mark's Greek is tekton, a builder, a craftsman who might work in wood or stone. Mark calls Jesus himself the carpenter; Matthew, telling the same scene, says the carpenter's son. So the hometown remembered a man who worked with his hands. Catholics honor that hidden work, and keep a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker. And notice: son of Mary, not son of Joseph. Readers have offered different reasons, and the text doesn't say. Third, the proverb. Jesus answers: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and in his own house, and among his own kindred." Fourth, the startling line. "And he could not do any miracles there, only that he cured a few that were sick, laying his hands upon them." Could not. Mark doesn't soften it. And he wondered at their unbelief. The people who had known him longest were the ones who couldn't see him.

If you pray, give thanks for them, as if they were new.

207.title: Two by two (Mark 6:7–29)
207.hook: the twelve go out with a staff and no bread; John the Baptist is killed at a party
207.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Passion of Saint John the Baptist on August 29, and the Church's missionaries and religious orders have long taken the sending of the twelve as a model of simple living; the sick receive the sacrament of anointing with blessed oil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carpenter, and a hometown that couldn't see him. Your line was familiar can blind. Today the twelve are sent out.

The extra charger. The spare sweater. A backup plan for the backup plan. Most of us pack for everything that could go wrong. Now imagine being told to pack nothing. No bag. No food. No money. One walking stick and the sandals on your feet. That's how Jesus sends out the twelve apostles for the first time. And while they're out on the road, Mark tells what happened to the man who went before them all.
screen: `PACKING FOR EVERYTHING.` → `SENT WITH NOTHING.` → `AND A STORY IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, two by two. Jesus calls the twelve and sends them out in pairs. Mark doesn't say why. Jewish law said a matter was confirmed by two witnesses, and there's a simpler reason too: nobody should walk alone. Second, the packing list. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he commanded them that they should take nothing for the way, but a staff only; no scrip, no bread, nor money in their purse". A scrip is a traveler's bag. Sandals, yes; two coats, no. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't hear you, shake the dust off your feet and move on. They go, preach that people should repent, and anoint many sick people with oil and heal them. Catholics see in that anointing a first glimpse of the sacrament of the anointing of the sick. Third, the story in the middle. While the twelve are out, Mark cuts away, another sandwich, to King Herod. John the Baptist had told Herod he had no right to marry his brother's wife, Herodias, and Herod had him locked up. Herod feared John, and liked to listen to him, though it troubled him. At Herod's birthday party, the daughter of Herodias dances, and the king, showing off for his guests, swears to give her anything. Her mother tells her what to ask for: John's head on a dish. Herod is sorry, but won't break his oath in front of his guests. John is beheaded in prison, and his disciples come and bury him. Fourth, why here? Mark puts the cost of the mission right in the middle of the mission. The ones sent out with nothing need to know how the messenger before them ended.

208.title: Come apart and rest (Mark 6:30–44)
208.hook: come apart into a desert place, and rest a little, then the crowds, then the loaves
208.howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand as a sign pointing to the Eucharist, and a retreat, days apart for prayer and rest, is sometimes framed with this passage as its invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, scrip, the bag the twelve left behind. Your line was take nothing for the way. Today they come back, tired.

Exams done. The shift over. The move finished, the guests gone. Then comes that strange hour, buzzing and exhausted at once, a hundred stories and no energy to tell them. The twelve come back from their first mission like that. They crowd around Jesus to report everything they did and taught. It's so busy, Mark says, with people coming and going, that they don't even have time to eat. And Jesus answers with an invitation, not a new assignment.
screen: `BACK FROM A BIG STRETCH.` → `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `AN INVITATION, NOT AN ASSIGNMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little. For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat." Apart means away, by yourselves. Jesus sees tired people and prescribes rest before anything else: an invitation from him, not a reward they've earned. Second, the crowd. They take a boat to find a quiet place, but people see them go, run around the shore on foot, and get there first. The rest is interrupted. And Jesus, seeing the crowd, has compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he teaches them. Third, the loaves. It gets late. The disciples say, send them away to buy food. Jesus says: you give them something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish. He has the people sit down in groups on the green grass, takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is filled, and they gather up twelve baskets of leftovers. Five thousand men were fed. Fourth, those four verbs: took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear them again at every Mass, in the words over the bread at the Last Supper, so this meal in the desert points forward to the Eucharist. And notice where it started: the meal on the green grass grew out of a break that never quite happened.

209.title: It is I, fear not (Mark 6:45–56)
209.hook: he walks on the sea and sees them toiling in rowing
209.howItsDone: Mark's account of the walking on the water is read at a weekday Mass in the Christmas season, after Epiphany, and Pope John Paul II opened his papacy with the words 'be not afraid'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kat' idian: come apart and rest, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was rest a little. Tonight the disciples row without him.

Three in the morning. You're pulling at something that won't move: a deadline, a sick child's fever, a relationship drifting backward however hard you work. Your arms ache, and you're pretty sure no one sees. That's where the disciples are tonight. Right after the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus sends them across the lake by boat while he stays behind to pray. The wind turns against them. They row for hours and get nowhere.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PULLING AND GETTING NOWHERE.` → `NO ONE SEES.`

segments.voice: First, he sees. He has gone up the mountain to pray; the boat is in the middle of the sea, and he is alone on the land. In the Douay-Rheims he is "seeing them labouring in rowing", with the wind against them. They think they're alone out there. They aren't. Second, he comes. In the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, he comes to them walking on the sea. Then Mark adds a strange line: he would have passed by them. Some readers hear an echo of the Hebrew Bible, where God passes by Moses on the mountain, and Elijah at the cave; in those stories, passing by is how God shows himself. Third, the word. The disciples think he's a ghost, and scream. Straightaway he speaks: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not." In Mark's Greek, it is I is ego eimi, which some readers also hear as I am, the name God gives Moses at the burning bush; the Douay-Rheims has it as I am who am. Heard that way, the words carry two things at once: it's me, your friend, don't be afraid; and, I am. Fourth, the boat. He climbs in, and the wind drops. They were astonished, Mark says, because they hadn't understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened. Mark's disciples still don't get it. Then they land, and people rush the sick to him on mats, begging just to touch the hem of his garment, and all who touch it are healed. Peter's walk on the water is in Matthew's telling, not Mark's. Mark keeps his eyes on the rowers.

210.title: From the heart (Mark 7:1–23)
210.hook: it's what comes out of the heart that makes unclean
210.howItsDone: Catholics hear this gospel at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the daily examination of conscience, reviewing words and actions and the heart behind them, is a Catholic practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I am: Jesus on the water. Your line was have a good heart. Today, an argument about washing hands.

The kitchen gets cleaned when guests are coming. The outside is the easy part. Then there's what comes out when nobody's performing: the comment under your breath in traffic, the text you send when you're angry, what you say about someone once they've left the room. Today, an argument about clean hands turns into a teaching about exactly that.
screen: `THE CLEAN KITCHEN FOR GUESTS.` → `THE COMMENT UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, the washing. Some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and notice that some of Jesus's disciples eat bread without washing their hands in the ritual way. Mark explains the custom: the Pharisees, holding the tradition of the elders, washed their hands before eating, and washed cups and pots too. This wasn't about germs. Some scholars explain it as a practice of holiness, bringing something of the Temple's purity to an ordinary table. A ritual handwashing with a blessing before bread is still part of Jewish practice today. Second, the challenge. Jesus answers with Isaiah: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." His example: a man declares his goods corban, a gift set aside for God, and so does nothing for his father or mother. The rule is kept; the parents get nothing. Third, the saying, to the crowd: "There is nothing from without a man that entering into him, can defile him. But the things which come from a man, those are they that defile a man." Later, alone with the disciples, he explains: "For from within out of the heart of men proceed evil thoughts", and the list goes on: murders, thefts, covetousness, deceit, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride. Fourth, how this is read. Mark adds a short aside, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "purging all meats"; some translations take it to mean Jesus made all foods clean, and Christians came to eat any food. Observant Jews continue to keep the food laws as God's commandments, and hear this debate as one among teachers. Catholics hear its center in the saying itself: in Mark's telling, what defiles a person starts on the inside.
screen: `A TRADITION OF CLEAN HANDS.` · `LIPS NEAR, HEART FAR.` · `NOTHING FROM WITHOUT CAN DEFILE.` · `WHAT COMES OUT OF THE HEART.` · then, large: `THEIR HEART IS FAR FROM ME.`

segments.voice: Think back over yesterday: not what you planned to say, but what actually came out of you, a kind word, a sharp one, something said behind someone's back. Don't argue with yourself; just look, then look underneath: was your heart tired, hurt, afraid? If you pray, offer your heart to God as it is, and ask for a clean one; if you don't, just notice.
Heart. Not just emotion, but the center of thought, will and feeling, where what defiles a person starts. Today's word.
Your line: out of the heart. Seven days: Legion, two daughters, the carpenter, the twelve, rest, the rowers, and now the heart. Day two hundred ten, in the book.
